newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: More unrest in Central Africa, France reinforces.
newsitem.headline: More unrest in Central Africa, France reinforces.

text.p: Four loyalist troops were killed on Thursday in an ambush by mutinous soldiers in Central African Republic where a five-day revolt has paralysed life in the capital Bangui, witnesses said.
France which ordered its troops stationed in the former colony to help maintain order has reinforced its Bangui garrison, the defence ministry said in Paris.
"The French contingent in the city now numbers about 1,500 men with the arrival of a company of reinforcements from our base at N'Djamena (Chad)," a senior officer told a news briefing.
French officials believe the mutineers want to overthrow the government and are in contact with opposition politicians.

The witnesses said the four soldiers were killed when they came under fire from mutineers on Singbes island on the river Oubangui, which disects the capital. Shooting erupted as the four approached the island in a boat.
Rebel soldiers held hostage 34 police cadets in Bangui on Wednesday, freeing them several hours later.

French troops have so far confined their role to guarding the city centre, the presidential palace, the radio and television station and other strategic points. They clashed with rebel soldiers repeatedly during a mutiny in May.

The mutineers vowed on Thursday to pursue their drive to disarm a civilian militia loyal to President Ange-Felix Patasse, who was away in Europe when soldiers embarked on their third revolt this year on Saturday. There has been no word on when the president will return.
The capital has been paralysed by a petrol shortage, with the city's main fuel depot firmly in rebel hands.
Prime Minister Jean-Paul Ngoupande, appointed by Patasse as part of measures to defuse the more serious mutiny in May, declared on Thursday that the latest revolt was political.
"This uprising, contrary to previous mutinies, was clearly politically-motivated right from the start," he told heads of diplomatic missions in Bangui at a briefing.
He said mutineers included people in civilian clothes. Opposition parties have condemned the uprising but at the same time denounced what they call Patasse's tribalist policies.

The army is divided between soldiers from Patasse's northern region and militants from the south, suspected of allegiance to former president Andre Kolingba who was defeated by Patasse in the first multiparty elections in 1993.
Kolingba's officer son, Major Guy Kolingba, was picked up at army headquarters on Monday by loyalist troops in what his associates term an abduction.

Mutinies in April and May were over pay and conditions. The May uprising was followed by serious looting in Bangui. France, which has defence accords with its former African colonies, deployed troops with tanks, helicopters and fighter planes.
Ringleader Captain Anicet Saulet issued a statement on Wednesday restating the objective of the rebels, who control the main Kassai army barracks and the capital's southern districts.

"The reason for the action of the military is to disarm the civilian militia and Codos (hired guns) of Chadian and Sudanese nationality. We will not lay down our arms until the completion of this mission," the statement said.
The mutineers on Saturday revived demands for back pay from 1992 and 1993 and for Patasse to revoke a decree ordering one of the regiments involved in revolts to a base out of the capital.
They also seek implementation of recommendations made by a national conference after the May revolt, including forming a professional army with a greater role in national life.
